newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Environmental insurance.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Environmental insurance.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Insurance professionals will gather in London tomorrow for an environmental insurance conference against a background in which European risk managers are increasingly re-evaluating their global risk finance programs.

In doing so, both they and their insurers should look closely at developments in the United States, where the environmental arena is marked by a growing number of industries transferring environmental risk and an increased awareness of the potential cost of environmental liability.

In addition the Securities and Exchange Commission is scrutinising corporate environmental liabilities, forcing company boards to limit or eliminate any indemnity for such risks offered along with property or asset transfers.
All this has created a need for cost-efficient insurance vehicles that shift environmental liability and clean-up exposure to insurance carriers, and a growth in competition has resulted.
Those competitors are now struggling to differentiate themselves in some way other than cutting the price, which they dare not do with such undefinable risks.

One response has been to provide customised programs and creative risk management solutions. For example, in connection with US federal 'brownfield' initiatives, which focus on the redevelopment of contaminated property, developers are now using new insurance products to facilitate the sale or transfer of real estate.

Other products now becoming common in the U.S. market include: business interruption as a result of a pollution release, mortgage impairment policies, and insurance for construction companies and their contractors for pollution events during projects.
Clients there are learning to test the competitive marketplace and compare the cost-effectiveness of various environmental insurance products.
Some are also becoming sophisticated enough to explore enhancements now available to manage the Total Cost of Risk, such as coverage add-ons, training conference, and claims mitigation.
Delegates from Europe and Britain meeting to discuss environmetal liabilities this week this should bear in mind two factors likely to affect them in the near future.

With the continued focus on voluntary clean-ups, brownfield redevelopment, and efforts to return contaminated properties to productive use, the debate will continue over the use of risk-based clean-up standards and "how clean is clean".

Secondly, the environmental insurance and reinsurance market leaders will continue to expand in terms of the number of players and available capacity. Underwriting flexibility will increase, and terms and conditions will grow more favourable.
As more and more industries come to recognise their environmental liabilities, evaluation of the total cost of environmental risk will become standard in risk management programmes.
